name: Bow and Arrow Choke from Russian Cowboy
description: Master the Bow and Arrow Choke from Russian Cowboy in BJJ. Learn collar grip mechanics, leg extension finishing details, and defensive counters from this back control variant.
summary: The Bow and Arrow Choke from Russian Cowboy is a gi collar choke that uses the position's single leg hook as a fixed anchor while a deep cross-collar grip stretches the opponent's body, compressing both carotid arteries.
overview:
The Bow and Arrow Choke from Russian Cowboy exploits the unique asymmetric back control to create one of the highest-percentage collar choke finishes available in gi grappling. The single-hook configuration of the Russian Cowboy already provides rotational control over the opponent's lower body, and when combined with a deep cross-collar grip, the resulting stretch between collar pull and leg extension generates tremendous choking pressure on the carotid arteries. The position's inherent leg entanglement means the opponent cannot simply roll or bridge away from the choke as they might from standard back control.

What distinguishes this variant from traditional Bow and Arrow setups is the pre-existing leg hook that anchors the opponent's hip before the collar grip is even secured. In a standard Bow and Arrow from back mount, the attacker must simultaneously manage hooks, collar grip, and pant grip while the opponent scrambles. From Russian Cowboy, the lower body control is already established, allowing the attacker to focus entirely on securing the cross-collar grip and transitioning to the finishing angle. The single hook acts as a built-in fulcrum point, reducing the technical complexity of the finish.

Strategically, this choke fits naturally into the Russian Cowboy attack chain alongside twister entries and calf slicers. When the opponent defends the truck transition by keeping their legs tight, they often expose their collar. Conversely, defending the collar grip by bringing hands high creates openings for the leg entanglement attacks. This creates a powerful offensive dilemma that forces the opponent to choose which threat to address, significantly increasing finishing probability.

injury_risks.injury: Carotid artery compression leading to unconsciousness
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate if released promptly; medical evaluation required if unconsciousness occurs

injury_risks.injury: Neck strain from excessive torque and rotation
injury_risks.recovery_time: 3-7 days for minor strain; 2-4 weeks for moderate strain

injury_risks.injury: Jaw or TMJ injury from improper collar placement
injury_risks.recovery_time: 1-3 weeks for minor injury; 4-8 weeks for significant TMJ damage

injury_risks.injury: Knee or hip stress from forced leg extension

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum to allow tap recognition
tap_signals: Physical hand tap on body or mat
release_protocol: Immediately release collar grip upon tap signal
Release leg extension and hooks simultaneously
Allow opponent's head to return to neutral position
If opponent was unconscious, elevate legs and monitor until full recovery
training_restrictions: Never spike or jerk the choke - apply smooth progressive pressure only
Never use competition speed in training rolls
Always maintain communication with training partner
Never continue pressure after tap signal
Beginners must drill position control before attempting finish
Always allow partner clear access to tap with hands or voice

attacker.name: from Russian Cowboy Attacker
attacker.description: Complete attacking guide for the Bow and Arrow Choke from Russian Cowboy. Learn collar grip setups, leg extension mechanics, and finishing details from single-hook back control.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the Bow and Arrow Choke from Russian Cowboy leverages the pre-existing single-hook leg control to simplify what is normally a complex multi-grip choke. The attacker's primary advantage is that lower body anchoring is already established through the Russian Cowboy hook, meaning the technical focus shifts entirely to securing the cross-collar grip and transitioning to the finishing angle. The key mechanical insight is that the hook serves as the fixed point of the bow while the collar grip creates the string tension, and extending the opponent's body between these two contact points compresses both carotid arteries simultaneously. Timing the collar grip entry is critical—the optimal window opens when the opponent addresses the leg entanglement threat, momentarily neglecting their collar defense.
key_principles: Secure the cross-collar grip before committing to the choke—premature extension without grip depth results in a jaw crush, not a blood choke
Use the existing Russian Cowboy hook as your primary anchor point, extending your leg to stretch the opponent's body and amplify collar pressure
Angle your body perpendicular to the opponent's spine during the finish to maximize the mechanical advantage of the stretch
Control the opponent's far-side pant leg or hip to prevent them from rotating into you and collapsing the choking angle
Maintain chest-to-back connection until the collar grip is fully secured—separation before grip commitment loses the position entirely
Time the collar grip entry when opponent defends the truck or leg entanglement threat, exploiting the momentary opening near their neck
setup_requirements: Established Russian Cowboy position with deep single-hook control under opponent's near-side leg
Seatbelt or over-under upper body control preventing opponent from turning to face you
Opponent wearing a gi with accessible collar material on the far side of their neck
Sufficient angle to reach across and feed the collar grip four fingers deep behind the opponent's neck
Opponent's near-side arm controlled or pinned to prevent grip fighting interference

execution_steps.description: Ensure your single hook is deep under the opponent's near-side thigh with your heel pulling toward your own hip. Establish tight seatbelt control with your choking arm over their shoulder and underhook arm beneath their armpit. Drive your chest into their upper back to eliminate any space between your bodies.

With your top arm (over the shoulder), reach across the opponent's neck and feed your hand four fingers deep into the far-side collar, palm facing up. The grip should sit behind the neck at the collar seam, not on the lapel near the chest. Pull the collar material tight to eliminate slack before proceeding to the next phase.

execution_steps.action: Transition choking elbow across the neck
execution_steps.description: Draw your gripping elbow across the front of the opponent's throat, pulling the collar tight against both sides of their neck. Your forearm should create a diagonal line from the far collar to your own chest. Simultaneously tighten your seatbelt connection with the underhook arm to prevent the opponent from turning into you during the grip adjustment.

Release your underhook and grip the opponent's far-side pant leg near the knee, or hook their hip with your free hand. This grip creates the second anchor point needed for the bow-and-arrow stretch. Without this control, the opponent can rotate their hips toward you and collapse the choking angle. Grip firmly at the knee crease for maximum leverage.

execution_steps.action: Begin the extension and angle change
execution_steps.description: Start falling to your back while simultaneously extending your hooking leg and pulling the pant grip toward your hip. Your body should angle perpendicular to the opponent's spine, creating a cross-body stretch. The collar grip pulls their head and neck in one direction while the leg hook and pant grip pull their lower body in the opposite direction, compressing both carotid arteries.

Fully extend your hooking leg while arching your back slightly and pulling the collar grip toward your own hip. The opponent's body should form a bow shape with your grips as the string. Apply steady, progressive pressure rather than jerking. Squeeze your knees together to prevent the opponent from rotating out. Monitor for tap signals throughout the entire finishing sequence and release immediately upon any tap indication.

common_counters.counter: Two-on-one grip fighting on the collar hand before grip is secured
common_counters.your_response: If they strip the collar grip early, abandon the choke attempt and return to seatbelt control. Use the opening created by their hand fighting to advance to truck position or reattempt the grip when they address a different threat.

common_counters.counter: Turning into the attacker and pulling guard before the extension
common_counters.your_response: Maintain the collar grip and follow the rotation. If they turn fully, transition to a cross-collar choke from inside their guard. If they only partially turn, use the collar grip to pull them back to the side and re-establish the Russian Cowboy angle.

common_counters.counter: Tucking chin and grabbing the collar material to create slack
common_counters.your_response: Increase the stretch by extending the hooking leg further while pulling the pant grip tighter. The additional body extension forces them to choose between protecting the collar and protecting against the leg stretch. If chin tuck persists, angle your forearm higher behind the ear to bypass the jaw entirely.

common_counters.counter: Shrimping hips away to relieve hook pressure and create escape angle
common_counters.your_response: Follow their hip movement with your hook while maintaining collar tension. Their shrimp actually assists the bow-and-arrow stretch if you maintain the collar grip. Extend your leg in the direction of their shrimp to capitalize on the added distance.

common_errors.error: Shallow collar grip that sits on the lapel near the chest rather than behind the neck
common_errors.consequence: The choke compresses the jaw and windpipe instead of the carotid arteries, resulting in a painful crank that experienced opponents will endure without tapping
common_errors.correction: Feed four fingers deep behind the opponent's neck at the collar seam, ensuring the grip sits at the nape. Pull all slack out of the collar material before initiating the stretch.

common_errors.error: Releasing chest-to-back contact before securing the collar grip
common_errors.consequence: The opponent creates space to turn, establish frames, or escape the position entirely before the choke is set
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant chest pressure against the opponent's upper back throughout the grip acquisition phase. Only separate your chest when you fall to the finishing angle after both grips are secured.

common_errors.error: Neglecting the pant or hip grip and relying solely on collar tension
common_errors.consequence: The opponent rotates their hips into the attacker, collapsing the choking angle and potentially recovering to closed guard
common_errors.correction: Always secure the far-side pant grip near the knee before committing to the extension. This grip creates the counter-rotation force that prevents the opponent from turning in.

common_errors.error: Jerking or spiking the choke rather than applying progressive pressure
common_errors.consequence: Risk of neck injury to training partner, and explosive application often results in losing grip control if the finish does not come immediately
common_errors.correction: Apply slow, steady extension over 3-5 seconds, progressively increasing the stretch. This allows your partner time to tap safely and actually generates more consistent finishing pressure.

common_errors.error: Extending the body without angling perpendicular to the opponent's spine
common_errors.consequence: The stretch pulls linearly along the opponent's body rather than creating cross-body compression, significantly reducing choking effectiveness
common_errors.correction: Fall to your side at a 90-degree angle relative to the opponent's spine. Your body should form a cross shape with theirs, maximizing the mechanical advantage of the bow-and-arrow stretch.

common_errors.error: Losing the single hook during the transition to the finishing position
common_errors.consequence: Without the hook anchor, the opponent can straighten their body and reduce the stretching force, making the choke ineffective
common_errors.correction: Keep the hook active and engaged throughout the entire sequence. During the extension phase, actively drive your heel into your own hip to maintain hook depth while your leg extends.

training_progressions.description: Partner in turtle, establish Russian Cowboy and practice feeding the cross-collar grip to proper depth behind the neck. No finishing—purely grip entry repetitions with partner providing passive resistance. Focus on four-finger depth and eliminating collar slack.

training_progressions.focus: Complete choke mechanics from established position
training_progressions.description: From established Russian Cowboy with collar grip already secured, practice the pant grip acquisition, angle change, and extension finish. Partner allows the sequence but does not tap until proper pressure is confirmed. Focus on smooth transitions between each phase.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 3: Chaining with Russian Cowboy Attacks
training_progressions.description: Practice flowing between truck entries, RNC threats, and the Bow and Arrow Choke from Russian Cowboy. Partner provides moderate resistance and defends specific attacks, forcing you to read their defense and transition to the appropriate follow-up. Develop the ability to recognize collar openings.

Positional sparring starting from Russian Cowboy. Full resistance from the bottom player. Practice the complete attack chain including setup, grip fighting, finishing, and transitioning when the choke is defended. Emphasis on timing the collar entry during defensive transitions.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Bow and Arrow Choke from Russian Cowboy primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The choke targets both carotid arteries on the lateral sides of the neck. The cross-collar grip creates a diagonal pressure line across the front of the throat, while the bow-and-arrow stretch compresses the collar material into both carotid arteries simultaneously. When applied correctly, this bilateral compression restricts blood flow to the brain, causing unconsciousness within 6-10 seconds of a clean application. The trachea may also experience incidental pressure, but the primary mechanism is vascular, not respiratory.

flashcards.question: Your opponent starts hand fighting your collar grip before you have full depth—what adjustment prevents them from stripping it?
flashcards.answer: First, tighten your seatbelt control with your underhook arm to limit their hand mobility. If they grab your wrist, use a circular motion to break their grip by rotating your hand toward their thumb—the weakest point of any grip. If they succeed in partially stripping the collar, do not fight for the same grip. Instead, release and reattempt from the opposite side, or transition to an RNC threat to force their hands up to their neck, reopening the collar. The grip fight should never become static—keep cycling between threats.

flashcards.question: What are the key indicators that the choke is properly set as a blood choke rather than a windpipe crush or jaw crank?
flashcards.answer: A properly set blood choke shows these indicators: the collar grip sits behind the neck at the seam rather than on the front lapel, the forearm crosses diagonally across both sides of the neck without pressing directly on the Adam's apple, and the opponent's face reddens noticeably within seconds. If the opponent is coughing or their jaw is being forced sideways, the grip is too shallow or misaligned. The stretch should feel smooth and progressive, with the opponent's resistance fading steadily rather than them fighting through pain.

flashcards.question: How does the Russian Cowboy hook function differently from a standard back mount hook during the Bow and Arrow finish?
flashcards.answer: In standard back mount, the hook primarily prevents the opponent from escaping laterally and provides positional retention. In Russian Cowboy, the single hook serves as the fixed anchor point of the bow—it pins the opponent's hip in place while the collar grip stretches their upper body in the opposite direction. The hook's rotational control prevents the opponent from turning into the attacker during the extension phase, which is the primary escape from traditional Bow and Arrow setups. This pre-established anchor reduces the technical steps needed to reach the finishing position.

flashcards.question: What is the correct release protocol after your training partner taps to this choke?
flashcards.answer: Upon any tap signal—verbal, hand tap, foot tap, or loss of resistance—immediately release the collar grip first to relieve arterial pressure. Simultaneously release the pant grip and retract your hooking leg to free the opponent's body. Allow their head to return to a neutral position without forcing any movement. Check that your partner is responsive and coherent. If they lost consciousness, place them on their back, elevate their legs, and monitor breathing until they fully recover. Never continue training until the tapped partner confirms they are ready.

flashcards.question: Your opponent tucks their chin tightly and grabs the collar material with both hands to create slack—how do you overcome this defense?
flashcards.answer: Increase the overall stretch by extending your hooking leg further and pulling the pant grip more aggressively toward your hip. The additional body extension forces the opponent to choose between holding the collar slack and preventing the stretch—they cannot do both. Simultaneously, angle your gripping forearm higher behind the ear to bypass the jaw entirely. If they maintain both defenses, use your free hand to peel their bottom hand off the collar by attacking the pinky-side fingers. The combination of increased stretch and targeted grip breaking defeats the chin tuck defense.

flashcards.question: When during the Russian Cowboy attack sequence is the optimal moment to initiate the collar grip for the Bow and Arrow?
flashcards.answer: The optimal window opens when the opponent addresses the leg entanglement threat—specifically when they use both hands to fight the hook or defend a truck entry. At that moment, their collar is completely unprotected. A secondary window appears when they flatten their hips to the mat to prevent the truck roll, which exposes the collar while their hands are occupied managing hip position. Attempting the collar grip while the opponent's hands are free and near their neck has the lowest success rate and should be avoided unless combined with a distraction threat.

flashcards.question: What are the most common finishing errors that turn this blood choke into a painful but ineffective jaw crank?
flashcards.answer: The three most common errors are: shallow collar grip sitting on the front lapel rather than behind the neck at the seam, pulling the collar grip straight down toward your own chest rather than diagonally across the opponent's throat line, and failing to angle perpendicular to the opponent's spine during the extension. A shallow grip causes the collar to press against the jaw and mandible rather than the carotid arteries. Pulling straight down compresses the trachea instead of the lateral neck. Without the perpendicular angle, the stretch is linear and generates compression rather than proper bilateral vascular pressure.

flashcards.question: In competition, what strategic considerations affect when to attempt this choke versus other attacks from Russian Cowboy?
flashcards.answer: Attempt the Bow and Arrow when: there is sufficient time remaining on the clock for a slow progressive application (minimum 30 seconds), the opponent has already shown vulnerability to collar-based attacks, and you have confirmed your collar grip depth before committing. Avoid this choke when: time is running short and a faster submission like the RNC would be more efficient, the opponent has excellent grip fighting and you cannot secure collar depth, or the opponent's gi collar is sweat-soaked and slippery. In IBJJF scoring, back control points are already secured, so the choke attempt is a low-risk, high-reward play from this position.

defender.name: from Russian Cowboy Defender
defender.description: Defensive guide against the Bow and Arrow Choke from Russian Cowboy. Learn recognition cues, grip prevention, escape techniques, and recovery paths from this back control choke.
defender.overview:
Defending the Bow and Arrow Choke from Russian Cowboy requires understanding that the danger begins long before the choke is locked—the moment the attacker secures a deep cross-collar grip from Russian Cowboy, finishing probability increases dramatically. The defender's primary strategic goal is preventing that collar grip from reaching full depth behind the neck. Once established, the choke becomes progressively harder to escape with each step of the bow-and-arrow sequence. The asymmetric nature of Russian Cowboy makes this defense uniquely challenging because the pre-existing leg hook limits the hip mobility needed for traditional back escape methods, and the attacker has one fewer step to reach the finishing position compared to standard Bow and Arrow entries.

Effective defense operates on a timeline: early-phase defense focuses on grip prevention and collar protection, mid-phase defense targets grip breaking and position recovery, and late-phase defense prioritizes immediate survival through rotation and guard recovery. Understanding where you are on this timeline determines which defensive tools are appropriate.
key_principles: Protect the collar as the first priority—both hands should address collar grip attempts before any positional escape work
Turn into the attacker rather than away when the collar is being fed to prevent the choking angle from developing
Control the attacker's gripping wrist with two-on-one before they can eliminate collar slack and commit to the finish
Use hip movement toward the attacker to collapse the stretch distance needed for the bow-and-arrow finish
Address the collar grip and the leg hook as connected threats—solving one without the other allows the attacker to cycle back to the choke
Recognize the point of no return: once the pant grip is secured and the attacker begins the extension, survival requires immediate rotation rather than grip fighting
recognition_cues: Attacker's top hand releases the seatbelt and reaches across your neck toward the far-side collar—this is the initial collar feed attempt
You feel the attacker's fingers digging behind your neck at the collar seam, pulling material tight and eliminating slack
The attacker's underhook arm releases and reaches toward your far-side knee or pant leg—this signals commitment to the bow-and-arrow finish
The attacker begins falling to their side or back while maintaining the collar grip, indicating the extension phase has begun
Increased stretch or pulling sensation on your collar combined with the hook driving your hips in the opposite direction

defensive_options.action: Two-on-one collar grip strip before the grip is fully seated
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately when you feel the attacker's hand reaching for or feeding into your far-side collar, before they eliminate slack
defensive_options.if_successful: Returns to neutral Russian Cowboy position where attacker must restart the choke setup from scratch
defensive_options.risk: Removing both hands from neck defense momentarily exposes you to RNC if the attacker switches attacks

defensive_options.action: Turn into the attacker and recover to closed guard before extension begins
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker has secured the collar grip but has not yet obtained the pant grip or begun the extension—the narrow mid-phase window
defensive_options.if_successful: Collapses the choking angle and recovers to closed guard where the Bow and Arrow cannot be finished
defensive_options.risk: Turning in with the collar grip secured may tighten the choke temporarily during rotation—must be committed and explosive

defensive_options.action: Strip the pant grip and shrimp hips into the attacker during the extension phase
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker has both grips but is in the process of falling to the finishing angle—last viable defensive window
defensive_options.if_successful: Prevents the full extension and collapses the stretch distance, buying time to address the collar grip
defensive_options.risk: If the collar grip is already deep and tight, closing distance may not relieve enough pressure to prevent the finish

escape_paths: Two-on-one grip strip on the collar hand followed by immediate turn-in to half guard or closed guard
Hip escape toward the attacker to collapse stretch distance, then rotate to face them and recover guard
Strip the pant grip and use the freed leg to establish butterfly hook, creating separation to work back to open guard

favorable_outcomes.how: Turn into the attacker before the extension phase, using rotation to collapse the choking angle and establish closed guard around their waist. The collar grip becomes ineffective when you are facing the attacker directly.
Strip the collar grip using two-on-one control before the attacker can eliminate slack and commit to the finish. This returns to neutral Russian Cowboy where they must restart the attack sequence.

common_errors.error: Pulling away from the attacker during the extension phase rather than closing distance
common_errors.consequence: Pulling away assists the bow-and-arrow stretch, increasing choking pressure and accelerating the finish
common_errors.correction: Shrimp your hips toward the attacker to collapse the stretch distance. Closing the gap reduces the mechanical advantage of the bow-and-arrow mechanics.

common_errors.error: Fighting the collar grip with one hand while the other hand addresses the hook
common_errors.consequence: Splitting defensive resources means neither threat is adequately addressed, allowing the attacker to secure the grip and maintain the hook simultaneously
common_errors.correction: Commit both hands to the collar grip threat first using two-on-one control. The hook alone cannot finish you—the collar grip can. Address threats in order of lethality.

common_errors.error: Attempting to roll away from the choke in the same direction as the hook
common_errors.consequence: Rolling with the hook assists the attacker's rotation to the finishing angle and may expose the back further for a tighter choke
common_errors.correction: Always turn into the attacker, toward their chest, to collapse the angle. Rolling away feeds directly into the bow-and-arrow finishing mechanics.

common_errors.error: Waiting too long to defend, hoping the collar grip is not deep enough to finish
common_errors.consequence: The attacker progressively eliminates slack and secures the pant grip, passing the point of no return where grip fighting alone cannot save you
common_errors.correction: Begin defensive action immediately when you feel any hand contact on your collar. Early grip prevention is vastly more effective than late-stage escape attempts.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that a Bow and Arrow Choke is being set up from Russian Cowboy?
flashcards.answer: The primary cue is the attacker's top hand releasing the seatbelt grip and reaching across your neck toward the far-side collar. You will feel fingers probing behind your neck at the collar seam. Secondary cues include the attacker shifting their weight to their side and their underhook arm loosening as they prepare to transition it to a pant grip. The tactile sensation of collar material being pulled tight against your neck confirms the grip is being seated. Recognizing these cues early—during the reach rather than after the grip—is critical for successful defense.

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to tap to the Bow and Arrow Choke from Russian Cowboy?
flashcards.answer: Tap early and clearly using multiple signals simultaneously. The safest approach is verbal tap combined with hand tap on the attacker's body or the mat. Because the choke compresses carotid arteries, unconsciousness can occur within 6-10 seconds of a fully locked application—there is a narrow window between feeling trapped and losing consciousness. If your hands are trapped by the attacker's grips, use verbal tap immediately. Foot taps on the mat are a backup signal. Never assume you can ride out the pressure or that the grip is not deep enough. The safe default is to tap when you feel sustained bilateral neck pressure that you cannot immediately relieve.

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available against the Bow and Arrow Choke from Russian Cowboy?
flashcards.answer: Three primary options exist depending on the phase: early-phase, use two-on-one grip control to strip the collar grip before it is fully seated behind the neck. Mid-phase, if the collar grip is secure but the pant grip has not been obtained, turn explosively into the attacker to collapse the choking angle and recover closed guard. Late-phase, if both grips are established, strip the pant grip and shrimp your hips toward the attacker to collapse stretch distance, then work to rotate and face them. Each option has a narrow window of effectiveness—recognizing which phase you are in determines which defense to deploy.

flashcards.question: Why is turning away from the attacker a dangerous mistake when defending this choke?
flashcards.answer: Turning away from the attacker during a Bow and Arrow attempt assists the choking mechanics in two ways: it increases the stretch distance between the collar grip and the leg hook anchor, amplifying compression on the carotid arteries, and it rotates your body in the same direction the attacker is pulling, accelerating their transition to the finishing angle. The correct response is always to turn into the attacker, toward their chest, which collapses the distance and neutralizes the cross-body angle that makes the bow-and-arrow stretch effective. Turning in may momentarily tighten the collar, but it eliminates the finishing mechanics entirely.

training_progressions.focus: Collar defense awareness and hand fighting
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes Russian Cowboy and repeatedly attempts to feed the cross-collar grip while you practice identifying the reach and stripping the grip with two-on-one control. No finishing attempts—purely grip acquisition versus grip prevention for 2-minute rounds.

training_progressions.focus: Turn-in mechanics after collar grip is established
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes Russian Cowboy with the collar grip already secured. Practice the explosive turn-in to collapse the choking angle and recover guard. Partner provides moderate resistance but allows the rotation when technique is correct. Focus on committing to the turn rather than half-measures.

training_progressions.focus: Defending the fully committed Bow and Arrow extension
training_progressions.description: Partner has both collar and pant grips and begins the extension. Practice stripping the pant grip, closing hip distance, and finding survival positions. This is the most dangerous training phase—partner must apply slowly and progressively. Focus on recognizing when to tap versus when escape is still viable.

Positional sparring from Russian Cowboy bottom against full-speed Bow and Arrow attempts. Integrate all three defensive phases. Track which phase your defense succeeds in and work to push your defensive engagement earlier in the timeline with each round.
